record.paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
record.original_question: Can phase-transition or statistical-mechanics models explain intermittent fluctuations in multiparticle production when it is uncertain whether such reactions satisfy the requirements for a pure equilibrium phase transition, and when heavy-ion fluctuations may differ from those expected from quark-gluon plasma formation and decay?

evidence.quote: This is precisely what people also did for the intermittency problem, connecting it to the study of fluctuations (both dynamical and geometrical) at a phase transition.
The main problem of this kind of studies is that one is not sure to meet the requirements for a "pure" phase transition at equilibrium for multi-particle production.

Even in the case of heavy-ion reactions a thermal transition from the quark-gluon plasma is not an evidence. On the contrary, the observed fluctuations in this case seem to be quite different from those expected from the formation and decay of a plasma.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In high-energy multiparticle production, "intermittency" denotes the power-law growth of normalized factorial moments $F_q(\delta) = \langle n(n-1)\cdots(n-q+1)\rangle/\langle n\rangle^q \sim \delta^{-\phi_q}$ of particle multiplicity counts as the size $\delta$ of a phase-space bin (in rapidity, azimuthal angle, or transverse momentum) is decreased. These scaling fluctuations have been observed in hadron-hadron, lepton-hadron, and heavy-ion collisions.

One proposed theoretical explanation interprets the observed intermittent fluctuations as critical fluctuations (both dynamical and geometrical) associated with a phase transition, by analogy with statistical-mechanics systems near a second-order critical point — in particular the deconfinement / chiral transition between a quark-gluon plasma and a hadronic gas.

Question: Determine whether a phase-transition or equilibrium statistical-mechanics framework can quantitatively account for the empirically observed intermittency exponents $\phi_q$ in multiparticle production, given that:
(a) it is not established that multiparticle production reactions satisfy the conditions (equilibration, well-defined order parameter, scaling near criticality) required for a pure equilibrium phase transition; and
(b) the intermittency patterns observed in heavy-ion collisions appear to differ from those predicted for the formation and decay of an equilibrium quark-gluon plasma.

Specifically, identify a statistical-mechanics or phase-transition model (thermal or non-thermal) whose predicted moment-scaling exponents $\phi_q$ match those measured across hadronic and nuclear reactions, or otherwise rule out such an explanation.
artifact.status_search_result: The literature reports partial progress: Lévy stable-law analyses classify intermittency patterns into thermal ($\mu<1$, QGP-like) and non-thermal ($\mu>1$, cascading) phase transitions, and heavy-ion data have been interpreted as showing non-thermal rather than thermal critical behavior. However, no single equilibrium-phase-transition model has been established as quantitatively reproducing the observed exponents across reactions, and the question of whether intermittency genuinely originates from a phase transition remains unsettled.

status_evidence.title: Levy stable law description of intermittent behaviour and quark-gluon plasma phase transitions
status_evidence.snippet: Levy stable laws describe intermittency patterns due to thermal (QGP) vs non-thermal (cascading) phase transitions.
status_evidence.claim: A Lévy-index framework partially classifies intermittency, but does not uniquely fix the underlying phase-transition mechanism.

status_evidence.title: Multidimensional intermittency analysis in ultrarelativistic heavy ion interaction
status_evidence.snippet: Scaled factorial moments in rapidity-azimuth phase space indicate a phase transition of nonthermal nature in heavy-ion collisions.
status_evidence.claim: Heavy-ion intermittency data appear non-thermal, differing from QGP-formation predictions, leaving the explanation incomplete.
